summary: When we were kids, our parents told us to: “Reach for the stars.” But what if reaching for the stars wasn't just a hopeful wish for a young kid? Inspired by turning the dream of a kid becoming an astronaut into an adventure, we built Path to Olympus. Path to Olympus is a free online game. Children aged 7-12 will learn what being an astronaut includes.  The game is designed with five stages of increasing difficulty (we organized them by Greek names: Hermes, Odysseus, Dioscuri, Hera, Apollo). First, they'll practice space walks in NASA’s huge pool. Then they'll float around in the zero-gravity plane and operate a robot arm on the space station. They’ll pilot a real rocket in space, dodge space junk, and survive on their moon base for 14 moon days. There are two bars at the top of the screen showing how much energy and oxygen you have; players will need to regulate these levels as they progress through the game. In order to give children a sense of personalization, at the start of the training, players can create their own astronaut. They can choose their name and customize their suit, visor, boots, and backpack. Throughout the game, Zeus Jr. (the helpful robot) will greet you by your name and give you fun factoids about what it takes to become an astronaut. After each level, you will be quizzed on what Zeus Jr. taught you. Finally, when you finish the game and arrive on the moon, you’ll become someone all astronauts are envious of: "a space master".
details: We wanted to focus heavily on accessibility; hence, our game has no downloads or sign-ups needed! The game can be played on any computer, phone, or iPad. All of your astronaut and progress information is stored within your own browser, meaning no personal data is stored. This focus on accessibility also inspired our intended game design: rounded corners and cartoon-ish text to appeal to children. Compared to other competitor games that train children to become astronauts, we add the unique feature of consequences. Our game shows the importance of regulation: astronauts planning their oxygen, sharing their energy, and hiding from storms. In order to build our site, we used a combination of JavaScript, HTML & CSS. Additionally,  three.js was used to create the worlds using WebGL. All of the worlds were coded from scratch with no models or images. In order to generate cohesive audio for our site, we used the Web Audio API to generate sound effects and a soundtrack. Vite helped us develop our game. Although we hosted our game on Vercel, we have additional relevant information on our GitHub page -> https://github.com/hariharv/Poseidon_13_NASA_River_Hacks. Regarding data, we used real facts taken from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency. Additionally, we used real solar storm data from the DONKI database provided by NASA. Some of these facts were collected using SerpApi.
